input.question: Why are the engines on small airplanes (e.g. Cessnas) make such a different sound than engines in cars that have a similar horsepower rating?
input.ground_truth: Some of the sound difference certainly comes from the difference in design and some of it is the lower rpm but most of the sound you hear from a small airplane isn't the engine, it's the propeller. To get an idea what I'm talking about listen to the sound of a turboprop like a Cessna Caravan, the engine in that plane is a turbine (basically a jet engine) so the engine by itself makes a high pitched whine, but the prop is so noisy that it drowns out most of the engine noise.

Question: Why are the engines on small airplanes (e.g. Cessnas) make such a different sound than engines in cars that have a similar horsepower rating?

Okay! Imagine you have two toys: one is a little toy car, and the other is a toy airplane.

The toy car has wheels and goes on the floor. Its motor is small and spins really fast to make the wheels turn quickly. That’s why it makes a buzzing or whirring sound that you can hear easily.

Now, the toy airplane has a propeller (like a big fan). Its engine doesn’t spin wheels; instead, it pushes air with the propeller to make the airplane fly. The engine sounds deeper and more “put-put” because it’s working differently, moving big air instead of just spinning wheels.

Real airplanes and cars are a bit like that. The airplane engine has to move a big propeller through the air, so it makes a different sound than a car engine, even if they have about the same power. It’s like singing “la la la” with your mouth closed versus open—it sounds different!
